solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Record start of tweet by a politician on X

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed on another follows it, so the earlier pieces come after

parts.note: the multiplication sign X is read as 'times'

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that single letter is kept

explanation.surface: A politician posts on X, the social network formerly called Twitter, and the tweet goes on record.
explanation.walkthrough: X looks like the platform but is the multiplication sign; TIMES then comes first because the rest sits 'on' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A timestamp is a recorded note of the date and hour something happened, so it works as a noun for a log entry.

clue.text: Rising bit of smoke's permeating support for lab kit

indicators.note: to permeate is to spread through the inside of something, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: the peg supporting a golf ball

indicators.note: in a down clue something rising reads from bottom to top, so it runs backwards

explanation.surface: Smoke drifts up from a stand holding laboratory equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support for lab kit' reads as one phrase, but 'support' is the golf TEE and 'lab kit' alone is the definition; BUTT'S turned upward sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A test tube is a narrow glass vessel used in laboratories, one piece of standard chemistry equipment.

clue.text: Source of penicillin doctor pulled out of odd places

indicators.note: letters standing in the odd positions are removed, leaving only the even-numbered ones

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of pulled

explanation.surface: A doctor extracts a source of penicillin from strange locations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled out of odd places' reads as extraction from weird spots; really 'pulled' is the source word and its odd-placed letters go.
explanation.definitionFit: Penicillin was discovered by Fleming in a Penicillium fungus, a growth commonly called mould.

clue.text: Lamp is put up over entrance

indicators.note: in a down clue what is over another piece sits above it, so it comes first
in a down clue putting something up turns it to read from the bottom, so it is backwards

parts.note: the verb en-TRANCE, to enchant or delight

explanation.surface: Someone fixes a lamp above a doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' looks like a doorway, which suits a lamp, but it is the verb meaning to enchant.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidelight is a small lamp, such as one at the side of a car or beside a door, so it is a kind of light fitting.

clue.text: Initially, hard to oust female feeling a certain desire

indicators.note: to oust is to push someone out and take their place, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: at first means at the start

explanation.surface: Someone finds it hard at first to get rid of a woman they long for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it is the whole phrase AT FIRST, whose F gives way to H.
explanation.definitionFit: Athirst is a literary adjective for thirsty, and by extension eager, so the desire in question is for drink.

clue.text: Bit of capital — one thousand pounds I invested in power firm

indicators.note: money invested in a business is put inside it, so these letters go inside the others

parts.note: the pound sign comes from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone puts a thousand pounds of capital into an energy company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks financial, but it is London; PIMLICO is a district of central London. The four letters I, M, L, I sit between P and CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A district within London is literally one part of the British capital city, hence a piece of it.

clue.text: Cut from blade, as some say

indicators.note: what some people say refers to pronunciation, here a non-rhotic accent that drops the r

parts.note: a sword is a blade, and in many British accents it is pronounced without the r

explanation.surface: A wound made by a blade, as people describe it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a past-tense verb, not a noun for a wound; the sound match works only for speakers who do not voice the r.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawed is the past tense of saw, meaning cut through with a toothed tool.

clue.text: Way to entertain little fool, perhaps

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one piece holds another

explanation.surface: A way to amuse a small silly person.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool here is a British dessert of fruit purée folded into cream, and sweet is the British word for a dessert course.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit fool is one example of a dessert, which British speakers call a sweet; 'perhaps' marks the example.

clue.text: Beat walls in vacated residence having sideboards

indicators.note: a vacated building has been emptied, so all the inner letters are cleared out
to wall something in is to enclose it, so one piece surrounds another

explanation.surface: A man in an empty house pounds the walls, his long sideburns flapping.
explanation.walkthrough: Sideboards are British slang for sideburns, not furniture. 'Vacated' keeps only the outer letters of a word, a common crossword device.
explanation.definitionFit: Sideburns are whiskers grown on the cheeks, so a man sporting them can be described with the adjective whiskered.

clue.text: Papers upset customer wanting upper-class periodical

indicators.note: in a down clue something upset is turned upside down, so it reads backwards
wanting means lacking, so a letter is left out

parts.note: a hotel guest is a customer
U is the standard label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: Newspapers anger a reader who wants a posh magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' looks like newspapers but is ID documents; 'upset' sounds like annoying the customer but turns ID round.
explanation.definitionFit: A digest is a magazine that summarises material, as in Reader's Digest, so it is a kind of periodical publication.

clue.text: Seconds required with some sterling seafood

indicators.note: what is required with something goes alongside it, so the pieces are simply set together

parts.note: a quid is slang for a pound, one unit of sterling

explanation.surface: Second helpings of seafood cost some British money.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is British slang for one pound sterling. 'Seconds' suggests another helping but is just the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Squid is a marine cephalopod commonly eaten, for instance fried as calamari, so it counts as food from the sea.

clue.text: Novel heroine and husband back call for clubbing

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so these letters are read in reverse

explanation.surface: A heroine of fiction and her husband come home and suggest a night out at a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubbing' suggests nightclubs; here it means beating with a club.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubbing someone is striking them repeatedly with a heavy weapon, which is a hammering or heavy beating.

clue.text: How toper opens more rum, swigging large tot

indicators.note: the manner in which a word begins is its initial letter, so just that single letter survives
to swig is to gulp something down inside, so one piece takes in another

explanation.surface: A drunkard opens another bottle of rum and knocks back a big measure.
explanation.walkthrough: A toper is a heavy drinker, and 'rum' and 'tot' both look like drink; rum means strange, and the tot is a small child.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is a very young child, the same as a toddler just learning to walk.

clue.text: Groups of new arrivals, tons entering during a film

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece is put within the others

parts.note: in means during, as in 'in the night'
Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and a kestrel

explanation.surface: Crowds of newcomers pour into a cinema mid-screening.
explanation.walkthrough: Kes is Ken Loach's classic 1969 British film about a boy and his kestrel, a favourite crossword stand-in for 'film'.
explanation.definitionFit: An intake is the batch of people admitted at one time, such as new students or recruits.

clue.text: Advanced runs to block improved team's attacking options?

indicators.note: to block a passage is to sit in the middle of it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a club improves its attack by purchasing a striker

explanation.surface: A football team strengthens its attack with players who make forward runs.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical phrase: a side that improved its attack 'bought forward', and R goes after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring a meeting forward is to move it earlier, so advanced and brought forward are synonyms in the scheduling sense.

clue.text: Oscar Peterson ultimately dotes on swinging solo

indicators.note: swinging music moves freely, so these letters are loosely rearranged
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

explanation.surface: Jazz pianist Oscar Peterson adores playing a swinging solo.
explanation.walkthrough: On one's tod is British rhyming slang: Tod Sloan, a jockey, rhymes with own, so it means on one's own.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something solo means doing it alone, which the slang phrase expresses.

clue.text: Linguistic flaw in news by newspaper head

parts.note: the i is a British national daily
a headland, as in Loch Ness or Orford Ness

explanation.surface: A grammatical error appears in a news report next to the editor's name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper head' suggests an editor; the i is a British newspaper and a ness is a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Using more words than necessary is a stylistic fault in writing or speech, a failing of language.

clue.text: Good-natured dope you heard is in love

indicators.note: a thing that is in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within
something heard is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: the letter name matches the pronoun

explanation.surface: A kind-hearted fool is in love, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' looks like an idiot, which suits the lovestruck surface, but it is slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous person is kind and giving, so both words describe someone of warm, unselfish character.

clue.text: Catch partner pocketing grand — it's won with tricks

parts.note: to catch an illness is to contract it

indicators.note: to pocket something is to tuck it away inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a grand is a thousand, abbreviated G

explanation.surface: A partner sneaks a thousand into their pocket after a crafty win.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a con trick, but tricks are the rounds of cards won in a bridge hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Contract bridge is a card game in which partnerships score by taking tricks, so it is a game won with them.

clue.text: Make invalid filling of lush doughnut, say

parts.note: to annul a marriage or contract

indicators.note: a filling sits in the middle, so only the central letters are kept

explanation.surface: A gorgeous doughnut's filling has been declared unfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' and 'doughnut' paint jam and pastry, but the doughnut is only an example of a ring shape.
explanation.definitionFit: An annulus is the geometric ring between two concentric circles, and a ring doughnut is an everyday instance of that shape.

clue.text: Jazz fan, in bed, lifted by ace composition

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting something up turns it to read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: jazz slang for a fan or player

explanation.surface: A jazz lover lying in bed is cheered up by a brilliant piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat is old jazz slang for a hip fan. The pieces simply line up: COT turned upward, then CAT, then A.
explanation.definitionFit: A toccata is a showy keyboard piece, often for organ, so it is a musical work or composition.

clue.text: Respectful gesture and awestruck remark for setter?

indicators.note: and simply adds one thing beside another, so the pieces are set side by side

explanation.surface: A solver bows and gasps in admiration of the crossword compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the crossword compiler, but it is the dog breed; the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Bow-wow is a childish word for a dog, and a setter is a breed of gundog, so it is one example.

clue.text: Finished postgrad degree with new supervisor

indicators.note: with means alongside, so the pieces are joined end to end

explanation.surface: A student completes a master's degree under a newly assigned supervisor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supervisor' fits the academic picture of a thesis adviser, but it is the definition of a foreman.
explanation.definitionFit: An overman is a foreman or overseer, especially in a mine, who directs other workers.

clue.text: Publication featuring King Edward's face and Mrs Simpson

indicators.note: a magazine featuring a subject carries it within its pages, so one piece holds another
the face is the front, so only the opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: A magazine runs Edward VIII's portrait beside Wallis Simpson, the woman he abdicated to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Wallis Simpson; the Mrs Simpson meant is Marge from the cartoon The Simpsons.
explanation.definitionFit: Marge Simpson is Homer's wife in the animated series, so she is literally a married woman with that surname.

clue.text: Officer getting popular, mature and tender

indicators.note: getting means acquiring more, so further pieces are added on

explanation.surface: An officer who is well liked, grown-up and gentle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' reads as gentle, the climax of a character sketch; it is the noun, as in legal tender.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal tender is money accepted in payment, and coinage is the metal currency issued by a state.

clue.text: Succulent core of plant supplied

indicators.note: the core is the very centre, so only the middle letter is kept

explanation.surface: A juicy plant centre is provided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succulent' looks like an adjective for juicy, but it is the noun for a fleshy-leaved plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The agave is a spiky desert plant with thick fleshy leaves that store water, the source of tequila; botanists class it as a succulent.

clue.text: Cooked fat eel and raw, small crustacean

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients into a new dish, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A menu offers cooked fatty eel alongside a raw shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raw' looks like the opposite of 'Cooked' in a menu, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The water flea, such as Daphnia, is a tiny freshwater crustacean that jerks through the water like a hopping insect.

clue.text: Inspiration for writer's books returning after long time

indicators.note: after means coming later, so this piece is placed second
something returning comes back the way it went, so it reads backwards

explanation.surface: An author's library books come back overdue and give inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: Erato is the Greek Muse of love and lyric poetry, so the writer is a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muse is a goddess believed to inspire artists, so Erato is a source of inspiration for poets.

clue.text: Club — United, say — regressing

indicators.note: to regress is to go backwards, so these letters run in reverse

explanation.surface: A football club such as Manchester United is going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' and 'United' suggest football; the club is a golf club and United is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedge is a golf club with a steeply angled face, used for short lofted shots out of sand.

clue.text: They may darn well see stars out to save millions

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe within, so one piece holds another
out can mean disordered or not in place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: People may darn well be dazzled when they rescue millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Darn well' reads as a mild oath, but darn is the mending verb and 'well' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamsters sew for a living, and darning holes in socks or clothes is one of the sewing jobs they may do.
